text.p: Base metal prices eased but gold firmed off its lows in quiet trading overnight.
Oil was little changed while grains prices were firmer.
The CRB index slipped 0.27 points to 238.72.
Business on the LME was slow during afternoon ring trading, with some profit-taking cutting into nickel's gains, while copper fell away as spreads eased on lending.
In copper, general lending this afternoon pressured the forward market, which eased back to end near the day's low at $2,177 a tonne, a $9 loss from Friday's kerb.

Earlier, nearby spreads again traded at or near the LME-imposed limit of one percent of the previous day's cash settlement, which was $24 on Monday. Belated borrowing on the previous day's prompt (tom/next) traded at the limit while the premium of cash over the next day was $23.

The cash/threes backwardation ended at $170/180 from around $225 at Friday's close. The continued impact of the backwardation is that there will be another LME warehouse stock increase on Tuesday, with traders anticipating a rise of between 10,000 to 15,000 tonnes.
The nickel market raced to a 4-1/2 month peak today, boosted by further speculative fund buying, with stainless steel output also expected to improve this year.
Total world output of stainless steel is expected to rise by 4.5 percent year on year in 1997 with a 5.6 percent increase in nickel-containing grades, broker Macquarie Equities said.

Traders say the discount on Russian metal is also narrowing as the market watches developments at Russia's Norilsk Nickel, where workers have passed a vote of no-confidence in management over wage arrears, but metals output is continuing.
Prices peaked at $7,740 a tonne, before profit-taking cut into gains and last business was at $7,670, up $85 from Friday.
Zinc notched up another two-year high today, building on the recent advances, although there was persistent resistance in the mid-$1,170s.

Traders are also waiting for developments at the AZA meeting in the U.S. The concentrate market is tight and European smelter sources told Reuters that MIM Holdings Ltd was cutting concentrate deliveries to Europe by half this year.
Last business was at $1,172, up $3 from Friday, but below the $1,176 peak.
The lead market hardly moved, with prices basically steady. Three months closed at $675, up just $3 from the previous kerb.
Aluminium stalled near the $1,640 level where there was expected stiff resistance and prices settled back to end at $1,626, still up $2, and just above the $1,625 chart point.

GOLD - New York precious metals were mostly higher as the complex steadied following last week's extension of the year-long downtrend in gold and platinum. COMEX April gold ended up $2.50 an ounce at $348.50, after trading in a $345.60-348.80 range. In the bullion market, spot gold was quoted at $346.45. "Gold held above Friday's lows, but would need to get back above $350 before anyone would get excited and the market remains concerned about potential European central bank sales," Pioneer Futures analyst Scott Meyers in New York.
GRAINS - CBOT wheat closed 2-1/4 to 1-1/4 cents per bushel higher on short covering after Friday's sharp losses.

OIL - NYMEX oil prices remained mixed ahead of the close Monday afternoon, with gasoline leading the way due to what some players said was decent buying activity in U.S. Gulf Coast spot gasoline markets. March crude was steady at $24.15/barrel.
